introduction: A pipeline can run arbitrary project code. If that code receives a deployment credential, its author can attempt to use the credential even when the value is masked in logs. This week makes that trust boundary explicit.

You will test variable scope with a harmless sentinel, separate untrusted MR checks from protected jobs, and draft the identity claims a future cloud role should accept. Actual AWS/GCP federation follows after you learn each provider's IAM model.
prerequisites: Weeks 9–10's private project, protected default branch and dedicated protected build runner are configured.
Work in ~/dev-opps-delivery. Keep all real deployment/cloud credentials out of this exercise.
Know your actual GitLab project path, numeric project ID and namespace ID. GitLab displays project/group identifiers in their settings.
If week 10 cleanup stopped the dedicated image runner, start it again on that VM with sudo gitlab-runner start before expecting protected build jobs to run.

concepts.title: Masking changes log display, not permission
paragraphs: A masked variable is still supplied to the job. Malicious code can use it directly, encode it or send it elsewhere. Protected-ref restrictions and environment scope determine which eligible jobs receive a value; code review and runner isolation determine what can execute there.
An untrusted MR should run tests without deployment credentials. A protected job still needs review because merging a malicious pipeline change moves that code into the trusted context.
concepts.example: A job can call a cloud API without ever printing its credential, so a clean log does not prove the credential was protected.
concepts.judgment: Ask who can modify the script and its dependencies, not just whether the variable has a masking checkbox.

concepts.title: OIDC exchanges a bounded identity for bounded authority
paragraphs: An OIDC ID token is signed evidence about a job, with issuer, audience, subject and other claims. A cloud provider verifies the signature using the trusted issuer's keys, checks expiry and audience, then evaluates the role's trust conditions. A short-lived credential is issued only if that policy accepts the identity.

The subject includes project/ref information. Stable numeric project/namespace claims can further constrain GitLab.com AWS trust where supported. Do not assume every self-managed issuer exposes identical provider condition keys. Authentication and the permissions granted by the resulting role are separate decisions.
concepts.example: A token from the right issuer but wrong audience or project must not assume your deployment role.
concepts.judgment: Short lifetime limits exposure; it does not excuse broad permissions or an overly broad trust policy.

concepts.title: Runner and environment controls form different boundaries
paragraphs: Runner protection controls where jobs can execute. Environment protection controls who may deploy to a named target where supported. Branch protection controls changes to a ref. None alone proves that all other boundaries are correct.

GitLab feature availability varies by tier and offering. Record which controls are enforced automatically. For unavailable approval controls, a documented release-owner decision is useful but weaker than a technical restriction.
concepts.example: resource_group serializes jobs for a target but does not decide whether their code or identity should be trusted.
concepts.judgment: Document the actual policy and exceptions, then exercise both allowed and denied paths.

steps.title: Map authority before adding another credential
steps.purpose: Draw contributor → MR test runner → protected image runner → registry → future deploy role → private environment. Label code-change authority, network access and credentials at each boundary.

explain: sed prints the complete current pipeline region without expanding any variables. Identify protected rules, runner tags, login and artifact transfer.
git log shows recent changes and who is reviewing the pipeline's authority in your workflow.
commands.expected: A reviewed list of each job's intended access, with no cloud key needed.
commands.troubleshoot: Do not copy runner config or .env into the threat model; record role names and scopes, not credential values.

steps.checkpoint: State which source changes could influence a protected job even if .gitlab-ci.yml itself is unchanged.

steps.title: Create a harmless scoped sentinel
steps.purpose: In GitLab Settings → CI/CD → Variables create DEPLOY_SENTINEL with value course-sentinel-not-a-secret. Mark it Protected and set environment scope private-staging. This is deliberately not a real secret. Keep the MR source branch unprotected. Add the probes below through a reviewed change.

commands.code:
git switch -c trust/scoped-sentinel || exit 1
cat >> .gitlab-ci.yml <<'YAML'

trust_probe:
  stage: check
  before_script: []
  rules:
    - if: '$CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"'
  environment:
    name: private-staging
    action: verify
  script:
    - test -z "${DEPLOY_SENTINEL:-}"
protected_scope_probe:
  stage: promote
  before_script: []
  rules:
    - if: '$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH && $CI_COMMIT_REF_PROTECTED == "true"'
      when: manual
  environment:
    name: private-staging
    action: verify
  script:
    - test "${DEPLOY_SENTINEL:-}" = "course-sentinel-not-a-secret"
YAML
git add .gitlab-ci.yml
git commit -m 'Verify untrusted and protected variable boundaries'
git push -u origin trust/scoped-sentinel
explain: Append two explicit probe jobs. trust_probe runs on the MR and requests verification context for private-staging; its test succeeds only when the variable is absent.
protected_scope_probe runs manually on the protected default branch and verifies the sentinel is present. environment.action=verify avoids claiming a deployment occurred.
test inspects values without printing them. Publish the branch, open an MR and inspect the negative probe. After review/merge, run the protected probe.
An explicit failure branch stops the sequence instead of letting later commands run after a failed prerequisite. Correct the cause and reopen Bash if the guard closed this terminal.
commands.expected: Unprotected MR cannot read the sentinel; the allowed protected scope can. Record actual job outcomes.
commands.troubleshoot: If environment protection denies the MR job before execution, record that enforced boundary separately; it is not the same as a script proving an absent variable.

steps.checkpoint: Explain what each observed denial/success proves, including any control that prevented the script from running.

steps.title: Write the future trust contract as data
steps.purpose: This draft records intended AWS federation claims. It is not a token verifier and grants no cloud permissions.

commands.code:
mkdir -p ci
read -r -p 'Actual GitLab.com project path, group/project: ' PROJECT_PATH
read -r -p 'Numeric project ID: ' PROJECT_ID
read -r -p 'Numeric namespace ID: ' NAMESPACE_ID
read -r -p 'Protected deployment branch name: ' DEPLOY_REF
python3 - "$PROJECT_PATH" "$PROJECT_ID" "$NAMESPACE_ID" "$DEPLOY_REF" <<'PY' || exit 1
import json,sys
from pathlib import Path
path, project_id, namespace_id, ref = (value.strip() for value in sys.argv[1:])
if not ('/' in path and project_id.isdigit() and namespace_id.isdigit() and ref):
    raise SystemExit('Use the actual project path, numeric identifiers and protected branch name.')
contract = {'iss':'https://gitlab.com','aud':'sts.amazonaws.com','project_id':project_id,'namespace_id':namespace_id,'sub':f'project_path:{path}:ref_type:branch:ref:{ref}','ref':ref,'ref_protected':'true'}
Path('ci/trust-contract.json').write_text(json.dumps(contract, indent=2) + '\n', encoding='utf-8')
print('Draft saved. No token issued or role assumed.')
PY
explain: Python prompts for your actual non-secret identifiers and validates their basic shape.

It writes the intended issuer, AWS STS audience, numeric identities and protected branch subject. This example assumes GitLab.com; self-managed installations must use their actual issuer and supported claims.
The file is a policy-design input for week 20, not a secret and not an executable authentication mechanism.
Bash read collects the four values before the here-document starts. Python receives them as separate quoted argv entries; its stdin is already occupied by the program text.

The documented default subject includes :ref: before the branch. GitLab's sample payload uses the string 'true' for ref_protected, not a JSON boolean. This draft assumes GitLab.com and an unchanged default subject; custom subjects and other issuers need their own exact reviewed contract.
An explicit failure branch stops the sequence instead of letting later commands run after a failed prerequisite. Correct the cause and reopen Bash if the guard closed this terminal.
commands.expected: A JSON contract matching one exact project and protected deployment ref.
commands.troubleshoot: Inspect the resulting sub field carefully. A typo can deny legitimate deployment; a wildcard can unintentionally admit other identities.

steps.checkpoint: Draft a separate permission list for the role. Trusting a job identity and allowing it to modify resources are different policy decisions.

steps.title: Exercise negative claim cases locally
steps.purpose: Use synthetic claim dictionaries to check your intended matching logic. This does not validate a real signature, expiry or provider policy.

commands.code:
python3 - <<'PY'
import json
from pathlib import Path
expected = json.loads(Path('ci/trust-contract.json').read_text())
def allowed(claims):
    return all(claims.get(key) == value for key, value in expected.items())
assert allowed(expected)
for key in ('iss','aud','project_id','namespace_id','sub','ref','ref_protected'):
    changed = dict(expected)
    changed[key] = 'false' if key == 'ref_protected' else 'wrong-value'
    assert not allowed(changed), key
    print('Denied synthetic wrong-' + key)
PY
explain: Load the draft as data. allowed checks exact equality for the intended conditions.
Each case changes one boundary while preserving the others, so a failure identifies an overly broad intended match.
These are design tests only; real issuer verification and cloud policy evaluation are explicitly deferred to the IAM implementation lessons.
commands.expected: The allowed synthetic case passes and every altered boundary is denied.
commands.troubleshoot: If a case is accepted, inspect which condition your draft omitted before writing cloud policy.

steps.checkpoint: Explain why decoding a JWT payload without verifying its signature would not authenticate anything.

failure.title: A broad environment scope exposes the sentinel to untrusted jobs
failure.boundary: Use only the non-secret sentinel. In GitLab temporarily remove its Protected restriction and set scope to private-staging as before. Rerun the unprotected MR probe; do not broaden any real credential.

inject.code:
git switch -c practice/sentinel-scope || exit 1
git commit --allow-empty -m 'Exercise the non-secret scope probe'
git push -u origin practice/sentinel-scope
explain: Create a separate unprotected branch and an explicit empty commit to trigger a new MR pipeline after the sentinel-only setting change.
Open an MR targeting main so the trust_probe rule applies.
An explicit failure branch stops the sequence instead of letting later commands run after a failed prerequisite. Correct the cause and reopen Bash if the guard closed this terminal.
inject.expected: trust_probe fails because the harmless sentinel became available in the untrusted path.
inject.troubleshoot: If the job is blocked by environment protection first, record that control and use the project settings audit as the scope evidence; do not weaken real protection to force the demo.

explain: Confirm the trigger did not alter application behavior. Inspect the sentinel's GitLab protection/scope settings and the test's exit status without printing its value.
investigate.expected: The difference is credential availability, not a source-code defect.
investigate.troubleshoot: A red probe is the desired detection signal; do not make it green by removing the assertion.

hints: The sentinel's value is harmless; the path it demonstrates would be dangerous for a real deployment credential.
Masking would not fix this availability error.

explanation: Restore the sentinel's Protected restriction and narrow environment scope. The untrusted job should no longer receive it. Review all real variables for the same mistake without exposing their values.

recover.code:
git commit --allow-empty -m 'Recheck repaired sentinel protection'
git push
explain: After restoring the GitLab setting, trigger a fresh MR run on the same branch so variable evaluation happens again.
recover.expected: The negative probe passes or is blocked by the intended environment control.
recover.troubleshoot: Retrying an old job may use configuration semantics you must inspect; a new pipeline provides clearer evidence of the current settings.

explain: Record the before/after trigger commits and the corresponding allowed/denied job evidence. Rerun the protected positive probe as well.
verification.expected: Both denied untrusted access and allowed intended access are demonstrated.
verification.troubleshoot: A policy that denies everything is not yet a working deployment trust design.

questions.prompt: Why doesn't masking stop a malicious job using a token?
questions.hint: Does the process still receive the value?
questions.answer: Yes. Masking changes selected log rendering, not the process's access. Code can use the token directly or transform it. Restrict which reviewed code receives authority.

questions.prompt: Why check audience as well as issuer?
questions.hint: Can one issuer mint tokens for different recipients?
questions.answer: Yes. Issuer identifies the signer; audience identifies the intended relying party. A token minted for another recipient must not be accepted merely because the signer is trusted.

questions.prompt: What remains unproved by the synthetic claim exercise?
questions.answer: It does not verify a signature, key rotation, expiry or actual cloud trust/permission evaluation. Weeks 20 and 39 must demonstrate real allowed and denied federation outcomes.

exercise.brief: Write a threat model and trust/permission draft for the future deployment role, including a negative-access matrix.
constraints: No long-lived cloud key or real-secret exposure.
Record actual feature availability and procedural fallbacks.
deliverables: Boundary diagram, sentinel before/after evidence, claim contract and least-privilege action/resource list.
acceptance: Wrong project, audience and ref are denied in the intended design.
Untrusted MR jobs do not receive the deployment scope.
The design distinguishes identity verification from permissions and from deployment approval.
hints: Include a malicious dependency or modified helper script in the threat model.
solution: Review every input to protected jobs, narrow identity and resource conditions, and define both positive and negative real-federation checks for the later cloud lab.

explain: Return to the known branch. Remove the non-secret DEPLOY_SENTINEL variable in GitLab after retaining the evidence, or leave it correctly protected only while the capstone uses the probes.
Never remove or alter unrelated project variables during this cleanup.
cleanup.expected: No real secrets created, and the sentinel is absent or correctly scoped.
cleanup.troubleshoot: Keep the trust draft under review; it is not proof of a deployed IAM policy.
